claims.text: Containerless electromagnetic levitation combined with rapid thermal analysis can accurately determine HEA melting temperatures.
The proposed method can accurately determine the enthalpy and entropy of fusion of HEAs.
High-speed in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction can quantify volume changes at melting in HEAs.
The combined approach can efficiently determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a diverse range of HEAs.
Post-casting homogenization removes microsegregation from vacuum-induction-melted HEA samples.
The specified homogenization produces a consistent starting microstructure representative of equilibrium solid solutions.
A high-vacuum environment minimizes oxidation during levitation experiments.
The experimental environment minimizes heterogeneous nucleation.
Heating and cooling rates of 10–50 K/s are suitable for capturing transient melting and solidification events.
Eliminating container-induced nucleation sites leads to more homogeneous melting and solidification behavior.
Suppressing surface oxidation leads to more homogeneous melting and solidification behavior.
Rapid thermal cycling and in-situ diffraction capture lattice-parameter shifts associated with thermodynamic transitions.
Containerless EML reduces heterogeneous effects that can skew thermal measurements.
Synchrotron X-ray diffraction provides real-time detection of structural changes associated with melting.
Thermal signals and diffraction-observed structural changes permit precise quantification of fundamental alloy thermodynamics.
Relative to crucible-based DSC, the method will measure melting temperatures and fusion enthalpies with improved accuracy and errors within 1–2%.
The method will determine liquid-phase properties and melting-volume changes with high temporal resolution.
Crucible-based DSC is more susceptible to container interactions, oxidation, and inaccurate detection of rapid transitions in complex multicomponent alloys.
The approach is most applicable to HEAs with melting temperatures between approximately 1000 K and 2000 K.
Convection and residual sample motion during levitation can introduce artifacts into thermal and diffraction measurements.
